title: Understand Your Shame
learningGoals: Notice shame without proving its story

deeperExplanation.question: What if shame comes from something real in my past?
deeperExplanation.answer: Your history can help explain why a moment carries so much weight. You do not have to dismiss it or prove it before exploring a response today. Begin with a manageable present example and ask what is happening now. If you want to work more deeply with painful memories, that can be a separate supported process. This short speaking experiment does not require revisiting your most painful experiences.

sections.narration:
Welcome. Today we are exploring Understand Your Shame. You repeat a word in front of someone important. Your cheeks feel hot and you want to look away. Then a thought arrives: they have seen something unacceptable about me.

In this session, we will separate event, feeling and conclusion, notice shame without proving its story, and continue with one meaningful sentence. I will explain the idea, show a visual example, and invite you to try it in a small experience of your own. You can ask me a question or switch to reading at any point. We will finish by choosing what, if anything, you want to take into a real conversation.

sections.narration: Shame often connects an event to a conclusion about the self. We will separate what happened, what you felt and what you concluded. The event might be a repetition. The feeling might be heat, heaviness or an urge to hide. The conclusion might be I am inadequate. These can arrive together so quickly that they seem like one fact. Slowing down helps you see the parts.

exercise.label: Guided rehearsal
exercise.scenario: You repeat a word in front of someone important. Your cheeks feel hot and you want to look away. Then a thought arrives: they have seen something unacceptable about me.
partnerPrompts: Please introduce yourself in the way you prefer.
Tell me one thing you care about.
What would you like to ask me?

sections.narration: The exercise is not to prove that nobody ever judges. It is to stop treating an anticipated judgement as an automatic verdict about you. You can also set boundaries with unkind people. A changed, unchanged or uncertain experience is information, not a grade. You do not have to report relief for this attempt to count as exploration.

sections.narration: After one manageable speaking moment, save an observation in the three-part format. Stop after a few lines rather than replaying the whole event. During focused practice, you can deliberately explore this one tool. In an everyday conversation, give most of your attention to the message and the other person. A familiar support can be available if it helps; you do not have to monitor the tool throughout the exchange.
